## Which comparison would you trust? {#d2s3-p01 .reader-slide .s1-review .d2s3-review}

The city did **not** allocate GreenWaste by lottery. Taking part followed the efficiency-score rule.

Matching selects comparison businesses that look similar to participant businesses on characteristics recorded **before** GreenWaste.

::: {.ask}
If two businesses look similar in the records, what can still be different?
:::

The outcome is annual waste management cost in **AED per business**, measured 12 months after GreenWaste. This city study is not the pilot lottery, and it is not the study of businesses near the score cut-off.

::: {.notes}
5 minutes. Retrieve comparison and population distinctions from DiD and RDD. Matching asks about participant businesses compared with selected comparison businesses, not the local jump. Start webR warming. Programme is equipment subsidies, installation help and training. Participants interpret, never write code.
:::

## How can we find businesses that look similar? {#d2s3-p02 .reader-slide .s1-review .d2s3-review}

<div class="review-grid"><div><h3>Business A: took part in GreenWaste</h3><p>Manager age: 45<br>Size: small</p></div><div><h3>Business 2: did not take part in GreenWaste</h3><p>Manager age: 46<br>Size: small</p></div></div>

::: {.ask}
Would you pair these two businesses? Give one reason, and name one thing you do not know.
:::

These profiles are invented for the activity. Do not open the reveal slips yet.

::: {.notes}
6 minutes. Two minutes individual, two pair discussion, two collect. Similar recorded features do not mean identical businesses. These two cards teach the choice, not the four-feature distance used in the city study. Keep outcomes withheld.
:::

## Find the closest comparison business for each participant business. {#d2s3-p03 .reader-slide .s1-review .d2s3-review}

Lay out the **seven profile cards**. Match participant businesses **A, B and C** to comparison businesses **1 to 4**.

1. Use manager age and size, and use each comparison business at most once.
2. Write your pairs and your reasons in **Q1 on worksheet page 3**.
3. Write which comparison business is not used. Keep the reveal slips closed.

::: {.ask}
Where is your pairing convincing? Where would you ask for more information?
:::

::: {.notes}
14 minutes. Distribute only page 1 of the cards (see the trainer print sheet). Optional seven volunteers with eighth group observing. Intended A2 B1 C3, comparison 4 unused. Ten minutes pair/record, four compare reasoning. Do not rematch on outcomes. Toy uses no replacement; full study permits reuse. This is a physical change of activity, not an additional scheduled break.
:::

## Reveal costs without changing your pairs. {#d2s3-p04 .reader-slide .s1-review .d2s3-review}

You now receive the **reveal slips**. A reveal slip shows what one business's annual waste management cost was 12 months after GreenWaste.

For each pair, calculate the **participant business's cost minus the comparison business's cost**.

Write the three differences and their mean in **Q1 on page 3**.

<button data-open="d6-toy" aria-controls="d6-toy" aria-expanded="false" data-closed="Check the arithmetic" data-opened="Hide the arithmetic">Check the arithmetic</button>
<div id="d6-toy" class="feedback" hidden>A-2: 900 - 1,900 = -1,000. B-1: 1,400 - 2,300 = -900. C-3: 700 - 1,800 = -1,100. Mean: -1,000 AED.</div>

::: {.ask}
Does this arithmetic show what GreenWaste caused?
:::

::: {.notes}
8 minutes. Hand out the reveal slips. Work one pair, then allow group calculation and reveal. These are invented costs, not city results. Correct subtraction is not causal identification. Unequal unrecorded influences could explain the gap. Pair choices must remain fixed.
:::

## How does matching work for the full city? {#d2s3-p05 .reader-slide .s1-review .d2s3-review}

1. Record **manager age, staff, premises area and filtration** for every business before GreenWaste.
2. Put the four features on a common scale.
3. For each participant business, select the most similar comparison business.
4. Compare annual waste management cost 12 months after GreenWaste, and allow a comparison business to be used again.

::: {.ask}
What does "most similar" guarantee, and what does it not guarantee?
:::

There was **no maximum acceptable distance**, and no participant business was excluded. Annual waste management cost before GreenWaste was **not** used for matching.

::: {.notes}
7 minutes. Explain standardisation as distance in city standard-deviation units, not four equal raw units. Squared distances choose a nearest neighbour; no propensity score is used. Matching with replacement differs from toy. Q2 page 3. Nearest is relative to available records; not necessarily adequate similarity. Transition to reuse.
:::

## One comparison business can be reused {#d2s3-p06 .reader-slide .s1-review .d2s3-review}

```{r, results='asis'}
html_out(d6_reuse())
```

**4,794 participant businesses were matched to 585 different comparison businesses.** The most-used comparison business appears **440 times**.

::: {.ask}
Why are 4,794 matched pairs not 9,588 separate businesses?
:::

::: {.notes}
5 minutes. OPTIONAL: this slide and the 'reused businesses count each time they are used' line on the next slide can be cut or shortened if time is short. If it comes up: 4,794 participant businesses were matched to only 585 different comparison businesses; the most-used one appears 440 times; the stacked sample has 9,588 rows but 5,379 unique businesses; each reuse counts again in the comparison mean; the interval uses clusters = business so the reuse is allowed for; matching with replacement is why the pairs are not independent. The diagram is an illustration; the counts come from the GreenWaste data. There are 9,588 rows in stacked matched sample but 5,379 unique businesses. Repeated controls contribute repeatedly to the comparison mean and require appropriate uncertainty accounting. Do not confuse a reused control with 440 separate measurements. Q2 page 3.
:::

## Did matching make the measured features more alike? {#d2s3-p07 .reader-slide .s1-review .d2s3-review}

```{r, results='asis'}
html_out(d6_balance())
```

::: {.ask}
Q3 on page 4: which gaps became smaller, and which difference remains?
:::

::: {.fn}
Difference = participant mean minus matched mean. The **city standard deviation (SD)** is the usual spread of that feature across city businesses. Dividing by it puts years, people, area and AED on one scale.
:::

::: {.notes}
7 minutes. OPTIONAL TO SHORTEN: if time is short, show the table, read one row and move on; the reuse point is repeated in the clustered interval note on the result slide. Reference table is worksheet page 2. The raw difference column is in each feature's own units (years, people, 100 m2, share, AED); the SD column divides it by the full-city standard deviation of that feature. Why we show it: raw differences cannot be compared across features (is 0.3 staff bigger than 3 years?), and the SD scale shows which gaps are small relative to how much that feature varies. Full-city SD is descriptive scaling, not a universal pass/fail threshold or standard error. Filtration mean is the share of businesses with a filter. Age still differs by about 2.97 years; before-cost differs by about 161 AED. Cost was not matched on. Similar means are not identical distributions or evidence that all bias is absent.
:::

## The closest available business may still be too different. {#d2s3-p08 .reader-slide .s1-review .d2s3-review}

```{r, results='asis'}
html_out(d6_support())
```

The chart shows **manager age before GreenWaste** in participant businesses and in all comparison businesses. The bars show the share of businesses in each age group, on the same scale.

::: {.ask}
What else would you need to judge whether the matches are close enough?
:::

Imagine a manager aged 45 matched to a manager aged 46, and another aged 45 matched to one aged 70. Both could be the most similar business available, in different groups of businesses.

::: {.notes}
7 minutes. The plot uses all comparison businesses, not only matched ones; see page 2. It is a one-feature marginal illustration, not a joint four-feature overlap diagnosis. The 45/46 and 45/70 cases are hypothetical, not claimed city pairs. Request distance distributions, weak-support regions and sensitivity to an acceptable-distance rule. No caliper was applied here. Q3 page 4.
:::

## We create the matched result in R. {#d2s3-p09b .reader-slide .s1-review .d2s3-review}

```{webr}
#| context: setup
#| autorun: true
#| include: false
#| echo: false
library(estimatr)
gw <- read.csv('evaluation_data_GreenWaste_simple.csv')
city <- subset(gw, setting == 'city')
# Standardise the four matching characteristics, then pick the most similar comparison business for each participant.
X <- scale(city[, c('manager_age','staff','area','filtration')])
participants <- which(city$took_part == 1)
controls <- which(city$took_part == 0)
Xc <- t(X[controls, , drop=FALSE])
twins <- controls[vapply(participants, function(i)
  which.min(colSums((Xc-X[i, ])^2)), 1L)]
```

We pair each participant business with its most similar comparison business, then run the regression. The trainer runs the box and the table appears below it.

```{webr}
#| echo: true
# twins: the comparison business selected for each participant (found in the hidden setup step).
# matched stacks the participants and their twins. A comparison business can appear more than once.
matched <- rbind(city[participants, ], city[twins, ])
# took_part is 1 for participants and 0 for comparisons.
# clusters = business allows for a comparison business being used more than once.
fit <- lm_robust(cost_after ~ took_part, data = matched,
  clusters = business, se_type = "stata")
# The took_part row is participant businesses minus matched comparison businesses.
summary(fit)
```

::: {.ask}
What does the took_part row compare, and how does clusters = business deal with reused comparison businesses?
:::

You do not need to write or run R. Q2 on your worksheet asks you to read the table.

::: {.notes}
4 minutes. Prediction first, then one Run by the trainer. Walk through the comments, not the syntax; participants do not code. The matching step (standardise the four features, take the nearest comparison business for each participant, with replacement) runs in the hidden setup cell; the box shows how the pairs are stacked and the regression. The took_part row is the mean of the paired differences: -1,029 AED, interval -1,200 to -859, as in the printed table on the next slide. The hand version is the average of the 4,794 participant-minus-twin differences. If the runtime is slow or unavailable, go to the printed table on the next slide within the same time.
:::

```{r, results='asis'}

  check.names=FALSE)))
```

::: {.ask}
Q2: explain the sign, the comparison, the period and the units in one sentence.
:::

This is the difference in annual waste management cost **12 months after GreenWaste** between participant businesses and matched comparison businesses. It is not a before-and-after change, and it is not a lottery estimate.

::: {.notes}
6 minutes. The table printed here is the one the box produced. H6-A section 2, page 1. About 1,029 AED lower annual waste management cost 12 months after GreenWaste among city participant businesses than among selected comparison businesses. Business-clustered robust interval accommodates reuse, treating matches as given. It does not fully account for match selection or unmeasured bias. Population is the participants, not every national business.
:::

## What changes when matching leaves out manager age? {#d2s3-p11 .reader-slide .s1-review .d2s3-review}

```{r, results='asis'}
html_out(d6_results())
```

With all four features, the gap in manager age is **`r fmt(match_A$age_gap, 1)` years**. Without manager age in the matching, the gap is **`r fmt(match_B$age_gap, 1)` years**.

::: {.ask}
Q4 (a) on page 4: why could leaving out manager age change the estimate? Why is a larger estimated reduction not necessarily better evidence?
:::

::: {.notes}
6 minutes. Same city, same algorithm, three rather than four features. Controls change, not merely a row label. Baseline cost gaps 161 versus 540 AED. No-age result can balance retained features while missing age. Difference does not reveal true effect; fuller analysis also has limitations. Do not compare interval widths as overall credibility.
:::

## What if motivation is not recorded? {#d2s3-p12 .reader-slide .s1-review .d2s3-review}

**Motivation is a hypothetical influence. It is not a measured GreenWaste variable.**

Motivation could affect whether a business **takes part** and also its **waste-saving practices**.

Matching on manager age, staff, premises area and filtration would not directly remove that path.

::: {.ask}
What would have to be true for the matched difference to show the effect of the programme?
:::

After we account for the recorded features, there must be **no important remaining difference that affects both taking part and costs**, and there must be enough similar comparison businesses.

::: {.notes}
6 minutes. Q4 page 4. Spell out no important unrecorded confounding; not proof or a claim that motivation actually drove results. Consistent measurement and no important spillovers also matter. Better measured balance cannot certify this assumption. Ask for selection process, omitted predictors and sensitivity evidence.
:::

Read **H6-A, the matching study summary (worksheet page 1)**, and Table B on **page 2**.

In **Q5 on page 4**:

1. In (a), write the main finding and the paragraph or table that shows it.
2. In (b), write the key assumption for a causal reading and the paragraph that states it.
3. Answer (c) after the question below, and (d) on the next slide.

::: {.ask}
Q5 (c): what does "every participant business was matched" show, and what is still unknown?
:::

::: {.notes}
8 minutes. Four independent reading, two partner comparison, two debrief. H6-A section 2 supports coverage/reuse/result; section 3 assumption; section 4 missing distances/sensitivity and conditional interval. No external full report required. Accept concrete consequential requests, not generic more data.
:::

## The estimate is above 1,000 AED. Is the whole interval? {#d2s3-p14 .reader-slide .s1-review .d2s3-review}

```{r, results='asis'}
html_out(d6_interval())
```

::: {.ask}
Q5 (d): explain the difference between "the estimate is above 1,000 AED" and "our rule of at least a 1,000 AED reduction is securely met".
:::

The interval includes values below 1,000 AED, so it does not show that our rule of **at least a 1,000 AED reduction in annual waste management cost per business per year** is met. Whether the causal reading is credible, and the full programme costs, are separate questions.

::: {.notes}
7 minutes. Negative difference interval -1,200 to -859 becomes reduction 859 to 1,200. Estimate 1,029 above rule but uncertainty straddles it. Interval is not guarantee, individual range, probability of passing rule or allowance for all bias. Allow act/conditions/request with defensible reason, not mandatory policy answer.
:::

## Four methods, four estimates. Why do they differ? {#d2s3-p17 .reader-slide .s1-review .d2s3-review}

```{r, results='asis'}
html_out(d6_forest())
```

All four intervals sit away from 0, so each estimate is statistically different from no change. They still differ from each other because each method compares **different businesses** and rests on **a different assumption**. They are not four tries at the same number.

::: {.ask}
Which would you trust most for a decision about the whole city, and what would you ask first?
:::

::: {.notes}
7 minutes. This is the first place the week's estimates sit side by side. All four show lower costs, roughly 700 to 1,030 AED a year. Lottery (pilot district): 1,014, interval 863 to 1,166. Difference-in-differences (city participants): 812, interval 792 to 833. Regression discontinuity (businesses near score 58): 721, interval 498 to 943. Matching (city participants): 1,029, interval 859 to 1,200. Two intervals lie wholly below our 1,000 AED rule (difference-in-differences, regression discontinuity); two include it (lottery, matching). Statistical significance versus our rule: all four intervals exclude 0, so each estimate is statistically different from zero, meaning GreenWaste lowered costs on every method. That is a different question from our rule of at least 1,000 AED. The lottery (863 to 1,166) and matching (859 to 1,200) intervals include 1,000, so the data cannot tell them apart from 1,000: the true reduction could be above or below the rule. The difference-in-differences (792 to 833) and regression discontinuity (498 to 943) intervals lie wholly below 1,000, so they are statistically below the rule, though close (difference-in-differences is about 19 percent short). If 1,000 AED is a hard minimum, these numbers alone do not support expanding. But every method shows a real reduction and all are fairly near the rule, so expanding may still be worth it once full costs and other benefits are weighed. The evaluation tells us what the data support; whether a reduction of roughly 800 to 1,000 AED is good enough is the commissioner's judgment. Keep the evaluation result and our judgment separate. Do not average the four and do not pick the one that suits. Differences come from three places: who is described (pilot district, city participants, businesses near the cut-off), what has to be true (next slide), and chance. Narrow intervals say nothing about the assumption: difference-in-differences has the narrowest interval and its key assumption cannot be checked with one earlier measurement. How to decide: start from the group the decision is about, then prefer the design whose key assumption is most believable for that group and ask what evidence would test it. The lottery is the benchmark only for the pilot district. Agreement across methods that fail in different ways is more reassuring than any single estimate.
:::

## What does each method have to assume? {#d2s3-p18 .reader-slide .s1-review .d2s3-review}

```{r, results='asis'}
html_out(d6_methods())
```

::: {.ask}
Which assumption is easiest to check with the data we have? Which is hardest?
:::

Choose by the assumption, not by the size of the estimate. Worksheet Q6 on page 4 is extra: try it on your own if you like.

::: {.notes}
6 minutes. Review slide for the whole day; one row per method, answers should come from the sessions. Lottery: assignment by chance held, few dropped out, no spillovers. Difference-in-differences: untreated costs would have changed by the same amount in both groups; one earlier measurement cannot test this. Regression discontinuity: nothing else changes at the cut-off and businesses cannot move across it; the estimate is local to businesses near score 58. Matching: no important unrecorded influence such as motivation; check match quality. Easiest to check with this file: matching balance on recorded features (partly). Hardest: unrecorded influences and parallel trends with one earlier measurement. Worksheet Q6 is optional extra work for participants, not a timed task.
:::

## Which method fits? Choose a path. {#d2s3-p19 .reader-slide .s1-review .d2s3-review}

{{< include _methods_tree.qmd >}}

::: {.notes}
10 minutes. Interactive decision tree for the four methods in this module. Read the question aloud, let the room vote (hands or Menti), then press the answer button; the path lights up and the end of the path is revealed. Use Back for one step or Start over to try another route. Suggested runs: (1) After, before and after data, similar earlier paths: difference-in-differences. (2) After, no before data, a score cut-off: regression discontinuity. (3) After, no cut-off, recorded characteristics explain taking part: matching. (4) Before, randomising is possible: lottery. (5) After, nothing fits: no credible comparison yet. (6) Before, randomising is not possible, no cut-off, before and after data can be collected for both groups, similar paths are plausible: difference-in-differences, even though no data exist yet. (6) Before, randomising is not possible, earlier and later data can be collected for both groups, similar paths are plausible: difference-in-differences, even though no data exist yet. Point out the note under the tree: it is a starting guide, other methods can still be possible (for example, earlier data and no cut-off can still be planned as a difference-in-differences), and many evaluations are planned before any data exist. Point out the note under the tree: it is a starting guide, the order follows how credible each method usually is, other methods can still be possible, every method needs enough data and a large enough sample, and evaluations are best planned before any data exist. The next slide sets the four methods side by side. Ask where GreenWaste's city evaluation would land, and what it would take to move it to another box. A static copy of the tree is on the website (handouts/methods_decision_tree.html, with a PDF and SVG). The tree points to the assumption each method rests on; it does not show the method was done well.
:::

## What does each method need? {#d2s3-p20 .reader-slide .s1-review .d2s3-review}

{{< include _methods_cards.qmd >}}

::: {.notes}
5 minutes. The four methods side by side: what each needs, what rules it out, and when it can still be planned.
